people.name: René V. Dawis
body: In the early 1950s, a young psychology instructor from the University of the Philippines arrived in Minneapolis to start graduate school. René Dawis would spend most of the next seven decades at the University of Minnesota, and his work there changed how counselors in the United States think about the fit between a person and a job.

Dawis was born in the Philippines on December 29, 1928, the son of a professor of agronomy. He earned his B.A. cum laude from the University of the Philippines in 1951 and taught psychology there for two years. He then came to Minnesota, finishing a master's degree in 1955 and a Ph.D. in 1956. In 1953, twelve Filipino University of Minnesota students founded what became the Fil-Minnesotan Association, and MNopedia names Dawis, with Lily Salcedo, as one of its early leaders.

His mentor, Donald G. Paterson, recruited him as research director for a federally funded study of how people with disabilities adjust to work. That study grew into the Work Adjustment Project, which ran for almost 15 years. Out of it came the Theory of Work Adjustment, first presented in 1964 and revised in 1969. In plain terms, work goes well when a person's abilities match the job's demands and the job meets the person's needs.

Dawis later served as co-principal investigator with Lloyd H. Lofquist. He headed the university's Counseling Psychology Program from 1975 to 1985, and in 1999 the Society of Counseling Psychology gave him its Leona Tyler Award. He retired in 1997. He published six books, advised 78 students through their Ph.D.s and consulted for more than 50 organizations. He died at his longtime home in the Prospect Park neighborhood of Minneapolis on January 11, 2026, two weeks after his 97th birthday.
keyFacts: 1951: B.A. cum laude, University of the Philippines.
1955 and 1956: M.A. and Ph.D., University of Minnesota.
1953: Among the early leaders of the Fil-Minnesotan Association.
1964: Theory of Work Adjustment first published; revised in 1969.
people.connectToWork: When your program judges whether a job or service is a good fit, whose abilities and needs are you measuring, and who gets to say what fit means?

people.name: Reynaldo "Reggie" Aligada Jr.
body: On May 19, 2026, the governor named Reynaldo "Reggie" Aligada Jr. to the Minnesota Supreme Court. When he took his seat on October 1, 2026, he became the first Asian Pacific American justice in the court's history. News coverage describes him as a Filipino American jurist.

His education and legal career are in Minnesota. He earned his bachelor's degree at Saint John's University in Collegeville and his law degree in 2002 from William Mitchell College of Law, now Mitchell Hamline School of Law. He clerked for Judge Wilhelmina M. Wright of the Minnesota Court of Appeals and for Judge Michael J. Davis of the U.S. District Court, and then worked at the firm Robins, Kaplan, Miller & Ciresi.

He spent much of his career on the defense side, at the Office of the Federal Defender in Minneapolis, which represents people charged with federal crimes who cannot afford a lawyer. He started as an assistant federal defender and became first assistant federal defender. In 2019 the governor appointed him to the Ramsey County bench, and voters elected him to that seat in 2020. He has served on Mitchell Hamline's Board of Trustees since 2019. As of October 2026 he sits as an associate justice.
keyFacts: 2002: Law degree, William Mitchell College of Law.
Assistant, then first assistant, federal defender in Minneapolis.
September 2019: Appointed to the Ramsey County District Court; elected in 2020.
May 19, 2026: Named to the Minnesota Supreme Court.
October 1, 2026: Took office as the state's first Asian Pacific American justice.
people.connectToWork: When a decision about a person's rights reaches your desk, what do you know about how it looks from the side of the person who cannot afford help?

people.name: Martin F. Manalansan IV
body: Before he became a scholar, Martin Manalansan spent about ten years on the front lines of the AIDS epidemic in New York City. He worked in HIV and AIDS research, program evaluation and prevention education at Gay Men's Health Crisis and the Asian Pacific Islander Coalition on HIV/AIDS.

His best-known book, Global Divas: Filipino Gay Men in the Diaspora, was published by Duke University Press in 2003. It is a study built on close observation and interviews with Filipino gay immigrants in New York. It challenges the idea that immigrants simply assimilate into one mainstream gay identity, and shows them drawing on Filipino language, humor and family ties while creating something new. It won the 2003 Ruth Benedict Prize from the Society of Lesbian and Gay Anthropologists.

When the book came out, Manalansan taught anthropology at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. He is now Professor of American Studies at the University of Minnesota, Twin Cities, where he holds the Beverly and Richard Fink Professorship in Liberal Arts. He has edited or co-edited five anthologies, including Filipino Studies: Palimpsests of Nation and Diaspora. His research covers queer migrants without legal immigration status, Asian American immigrant food, and how care works among immigrants.
keyFacts: About ten years in HIV and AIDS research and prevention in New York City before academia.
Current: endowed professor of American Studies, University of Minnesota, Twin Cities.
people.connectToWork: Who cares for the people you serve outside any formal program, and does your process have a way to see that care when those people are not relatives on paper?

people.name: Larry Itliong
body: On September 8, 1965, Filipino farmworkers met in Delano, California, and voted to walk out of the grape fields. They were led by Larry Itliong of the AFL-CIO's Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee. About 1,500 workers struck. Days later, Cesar Chavez's mostly Mexican American National Farm Workers Association joined them. Together they carried the Delano grape strike and boycott.

Itliong was born on October 25, 1913, in Pangasinan, Philippines, then a U.S. territory, and came to the United States in 1929, at 15. He belonged to the generation known as the Manongs, an Ilocano word of respect for older brothers. They were mostly young Filipino men who worked in the fields of California and Washington and in Alaska salmon canneries. Laws against interracial marriage and limits on Filipino immigration left many of them without families of their own.

He joined his first strike in 1930 near Monroe, Washington, later organized in the Salinas Valley and helped lead the 1948 Stockton asparagus strike. He lost three fingers in a work accident, and accounts differ on where, which earned him the nickname Seven Fingers. In 1967 the two unions merged into the United Farm Workers, with Itliong as assistant director. He resigned in 1971. He helped create Agbayani Village, a retirement home for aging Manongs that opened in 1974, and died in Delano on February 8, 1977.
Since 2015, California has marked October 25 as Larry Itliong Day.
keyFacts: September 8, 1965: Led the Filipino walkout that began the Delano grape strike.
1967: Became assistant director of the United Farm Workers; resigned in 1971.
people.connectToWork: When your team tells the history of a program or a change, whose work has been left out of the story, and how would you find out?

people.name: Philip Vera Cruz
body: In 1977, Cesar Chavez accepted an invitation to visit the Philippines from its president, Ferdinand Marcos, who had imposed martial law in 1972. Philip Vera Cruz, a vice president of the United Farm Workers, objected and left the union he had helped build.

Vera Cruz was born in Saoang, San Juan, Ilocos Sur, and entered the United States through Seattle in 1926, at 20. He briefly studied at Gonzaga University in 1931 before work ended his schooling. In 1934, the Tydings-McDuffie Act reclassified Filipinos as aliens and sharply limited Filipino immigration. He was drafted in 1942 and served in the 2nd Filipino Infantry Regiment until he was discharged because of his age.

After the war he did seasonal farm work in the San Joaquin Valley and joined the 1948 Stockton asparagus strike. He was part of the September 8, 1965, vote that started the Delano grape strike and became a UFW vice president after the 1967 merger. He also helped build the Paulo Agbayani Retirement Village, which opened in 1974 so that aging Filipino farmworkers with no families nearby would have a home.

In 1987 he received the Ninoy M. Aquino Award and returned to the Philippines for the first time since 1926. He died in Bakersfield in June 1994. NBC News reported in December 2015 that Alvarado Middle School in Union City, California, was being renamed Itliong-Vera Cruz Middle School, reported as the first U.S. school named for Filipino Americans.
keyFacts: 1942: Drafted into the 2nd Filipino Infantry Regiment.
September 8, 1965: Took part in the Delano strike vote.
1977: Left the UFW after Chavez's trip to Marcos's Philippines.
people.connectToWork: What might a person's ties to politics or family in another country mean for what they need from your service, and how could you ask without assuming?

people.name: Carlos Bulosan
body: In March 1943, readers of The Saturday Evening Post found Norman Rockwell's painting Freedom from Want next to an essay by Carlos Bulosan, a Filipino migrant laborer writing about freedoms people like him were often denied. The essay made him famous.

Bulosan was born in Binalonan, Pangasinan. Sources disagree on the year, and his baptismal record gives 1911. He sailed for America in 1930 and never returned home. He worked in fields and canneries along the West Coast and faced racist violence and exclusion. Starting in 1936 he spent about two years in a Los Angeles hospital with tuberculosis, reading and writing there.

His books include Letter from America (1942), The Laughter of My Father (1944) and America Is in the Heart (1946), a semi-autobiographical novel about Filipino migrant life. In 1952 he edited the yearbook of ILWU Local 37, the Seattle cannery workers' union. During the Red Scare he was blacklisted and watched by the FBI. He died in Seattle on September 11, 1956, of pneumonia complicated by tuberculosis. Admirers raised money for a headstone in 1982.
In 1973 the University of Washington Press republished America Is in the Heart for a new generation of readers.
keyFacts: 1946: America Is in the Heart published.
1973: America Is in the Heart republished.
people.connectToWork: Illness and years of low-wage work shaped how Bulosan lived and wrote. When you read a person's record, what does it leave out about what they have been through and what they have made of it?

people.name: Vicki Manalo Draves
body: On August 3, 1948, at the London Olympics, Vicki Draves won gold in the women's 3-meter springboard. Days later she won the 10-meter platform as well. By the Associated Press's account she was the first woman to win two diving golds at the same Olympics, and Google's tribute calls her the first Asian American woman to win an Olympic medal.

She was born Victoria Manalo in San Francisco on December 31, 1924. Her father, a Filipino immigrant, was a chef and musician, and her mother, Gertrude Taylor, was English. Facing prejudice against Filipinos at the area's swim clubs, she competed under her mother's maiden name, as Vicki Taylor. She won three straight U.S. national platform titles before the Olympics.

After the Olympics she turned professional and performed in diving shows. She married her coach, Lyle Draves, in 1946. She entered the International Swimming Hall of Fame in 1969. San Francisco's Victoria Manalo Draves Park opened in 2006 at the site of her former elementary school. She died on April 11, 2010, in Palm Springs, California.
keyFacts: August 1948: Olympic golds in springboard and platform, London.
April 11, 2010: Died in Palm Springs, California.
people.connectToWork: Draves competed under another name to be let in. What might people in your system leave off a form or change about themselves to get through the door, and what would tell you?

sources.label: EBSCO Research Starters, Victoria Manalo Draves

photo.alt: Black-and-white photograph of Vicki Draves in a white swimsuit, smiling, resting her hands on the edge of a pool with children in the water behind her.

people.name: Antonio M. Taguba
body: In 2004, Army Major General Antonio Taguba was ordered to investigate reports of prisoner abuse at Abu Ghraib prison in Iraq. His report documented the abuses in plain terms. It was leaked and published that year. Taguba later turned the same insistence on an honest record toward another cause: getting the United States to recognize Filipino soldiers who fought for it in World War II.

Taguba was born on October 31, 1950, in Sampaloc, Manila, and spent his first ten years there. His father, Tomas Taguba, was a career Army soldier who retired as a sergeant first class. The Philippines was a U.S. territory in 1941, and NBC News reports that some 260,000 Filipinos served with U.S. forces against Japan. The Rescission Act of 1946 then denied most of them the veterans' benefits other U.S. soldiers received.

The family moved to Hawaii in 1961. He graduated from Leilehua High School and from Idaho State University in 1972, and joined the Army. In 34 years on active duty he served in the United States, South Korea, Germany and Kuwait, and he became the second Philippine-born U.S. citizen promoted to general in the Army. He retired in January 2007.

He became chairman of the Filipino Veterans Recognition and Education Project, which led a national campaign for a Congressional Gold Medal for Filipino World War II veterans. President Barack Obama signed the medal bill in December 2016. As of April 2026 Taguba was still the group's chairman, speaking at the Philippine Embassy's Araw ng Kagitingan (Day of Valor) memorial. He also chairs the board of Pan-Pacific American Leaders and Mentors.
keyFacts: 1972: Graduated from Idaho State University and joined the Army.
2004: Wrote the Army's Abu Ghraib investigation report.
December 2016: Congressional Gold Medal Act for Filipino World War II veterans signed.
people.connectToWork: When an older person's eligibility depends on old service or work records, what would you do if the system that should hold those records was built to leave them out?

people.name: Zenei Triunfo-Cortez
body: In 1990, a bedside nurse at Kaiser Permanente South San Francisco Medical Center was denied a transfer that she believed was discriminatory. Zenei Triunfo-Cortez fought it and won. In 2018 she became the first Filipina president of National Nurses United, the national registered nurses' union.

The American colonial government set up nursing schools in the Philippines in the early 1900s, and U.S. hospitals later recruited Filipino nurses in large numbers. In a 2023 post, National Nurses United puts Filipino nurses at 4 percent of all U.S. registered nurses and 18.4 percent of California's.

Triunfo-Cortez joined the California Nurses Association in 1981 and became a leader on the Kaiser Northern California bargaining team in 1998. In 2007 she became the first Filipina president of the California Nurses Association/National Nurses Organizing Committee. She kept working as a nurse while she led.

During COVID-19, she and the union pushed for protective equipment and safe staffing. The union's own count, which it says rests on limited race and ethnicity data, found Filipino nurses accounted for 21 percent of registered nurse COVID-19 deaths it recorded and 43.5 percent of those deaths among nurses of color. In October 2023 she stepped down as California president after 16 years, with Michelle Gutierrez Vo succeeding her. The union then said she would serve another year as a national president; its leadership page, checked in October 2026, no longer lists her among its presidents.
keyFacts: 1990: Won a fight against a transfer denial at Kaiser South San Francisco.
2007: First Filipina president of the California union.
2018: First Filipina president of National Nurses United.
October 2023: Stepped down as California president after 16 years.
people.connectToWork: Who on your team or among your partners may have lived through the worst of COVID-19 as frontline workers, and what would it take to include that in how you plan workforce or health outreach?

people.name: Jose Antonio Vargas
body: Jose Antonio Vargas grew up in Mountain View, California, and for years lived there without legal immigration status, a fact he kept secret until 2011. He was born in Antipolo, in the Philippines, and at 12 his mother sent him to California to live with his grandparents. He graduated from Mountain View High School in 2000 and San Francisco State University in 2004.

He built a career as a journalist while keeping his status secret. In 2008, at 27, he shared the Pulitzer Prize for Breaking News Reporting with the Washington Post team that covered the April 2007 Virginia Tech shootings. In 2011 he revealed that he was undocumented in an essay in The New York Times Magazine. He went on to found Define American, a nonprofit that tells immigrant stories, and in 2012 appeared on the cover of Time with other undocumented immigrants.

He directed Documented (2013), a film about his own life that aired on CNN, and his memoir, Dear America: Notes of an Undocumented Citizen, came out in 2018. As of October 2026 his own site describes him as the founder of Define American and host of its show and podcast.
keyFacts: 1981: Born in Antipolo, Philippines; raised in Mountain View from 12.
2008: Shared the Pulitzer Prize for Breaking News Reporting.
people.connectToWork: What does your process require a person to disclose about immigration status, and does the person know what will happen to that information before they answer?

people.name: Loida Nicolas Lewis
body: In 1993, the businessman Reginald F. Lewis died. He had built TLC Beatrice International, and AALBC describes him as the first Black billion-dollar dealmaker. His widow, Loida Nicolas Lewis, a Filipina immigration lawyer, took over as chair and CEO.

She comes from Sorsogon, at the southern tip of Luzon. She studied at St. Theresa's College and the University of the Philippines College of Law and passed the Philippine bar in 1968. She met Reginald Lewis on a blind date on a trip to New York, and they married in Manila in 1969. In 1974 she passed the New York bar without attending a U.S. law school. Hawaii News Now describes her as the first Asian and Filipino woman to do so.

When the U.S. Immigration and Naturalization Service did not hire her, she sued and won. In 1978 she became the first Filipina in the continental U.S. to serve as a general attorney at the agency, and she spent ten years there. She co-wrote How to Get a Green Card, now in its 12th edition.

She led TLC Beatrice through 2000; by her account, sales grew from $1.5 billion to $2.2 billion. As of October 2026 she chairs the Reginald F. Lewis Foundation, which has funded scholarships and microfinancing for Filipino families. She co-founded the Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund and, in 1997, the National Federation of Filipino American Associations, where she is chair emeritus. Carnegie Corporation of New York named her a Great Immigrant in 2008.
keyFacts: 1978: Began ten years as a general attorney at the Immigration and Naturalization Service.
1993: Became chair and CEO of TLC Beatrice.
1997: Co-founded the National Federation of Filipino American Associations.
people.connectToWork: What training or credentials from another country might the people you serve or hire already hold, and does your process have a way to see them?

people.name: Diosdado "Dado" Banatao
body: As a boy in Iguig, a farming town in Cagayan province in the northern Philippines, Dado Banatao walked barefoot to school. Decades later he helped build the chip industry of Silicon Valley.

Banatao was born on May 23, 1946, the son of Salvador Banatao, a rice farmer. He graduated cum laude in electrical engineering from the Mapúa Institute of Technology in Manila and trained as a pilot for Philippine Airlines before Boeing hired him as a design engineer. He finished a master's degree at Stanford University in 1972.

In Silicon Valley he worked at National Semiconductor, Intersil and Commodore. In 1981, at Seeq Technology, he put an Ethernet controller on a single chip. He then started Mostron in 1984, Chips and Technologies in 1985, and S3 Graphics in 1989. Intel bought Chips and Technologies in 1996. In 2000 he founded Tallwood Venture Capital.

He founded the Philippine Development Foundation, known as PhilDev, which supports young Filipinos in science, technology, engineering and math through scholarships, and he set up a computer center at his old grade school. He received the Ellis Island Medal of Honor. He died at Stanford, California, on December 25, 2025, at 79, after complications from a neurological disorder.
keyFacts: 1981: Put an Ethernet controller on a single chip.
1984, 1985, 1989: Started Mostron, Chips and Technologies, and S3 Graphics.
people.connectToWork: When you look at a person's starting point, what are you assuming about where they can go, and what would your program do differently if you asked them instead?

people.name: Cristeta Comerford
body: In August 2005, First Lady Laura Bush named Cristeta Comerford executive chef of the White House. She was the first woman to hold the job and the first person of color. She ran the White House kitchen for nearly two decades.

Comerford was born Cristeta Gomez Pasia on October 27, 1962, in Sampaloc, Manila, and grew up with 10 siblings. She went to Manila Science High School and studied food technology at the University of the Philippines Diliman before moving to the United States at 23 to join family in Chicago. She worked in hotel kitchens in Chicago, spent six months in a Vienna kitchen, and then cooked in hotel restaurants in Washington, D.C.

In 1995, executive chef Walter Scheib III hired her as an assistant chef in the Clinton White House. In the top job she planned family meals and designed menus for state dinners, receptions and holiday events. Michelle Obama chose to keep her in 2009. Her last state dinner was in May 2024, for Kenyan President William Ruto. She retired in July 2024 after serving five presidents and nearly 30 years in the White House.
keyFacts: 1995: Hired as assistant chef at the White House.
July 2024: Retired after serving five presidents.
people.connectToWork: How do people from outside the usual pipeline move up in your organization, and who notices their skill along the way?

people.name: Robert Lopez
body: In March 2018, Robert Lopez and his wife, Kristen Anderson-Lopez, won the Academy Award for Best Original Song for "Remember Me" from the Pixar film Coco. With that win, Lopez became the first person to win at least two each of the Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony, sometimes called the double EGOT.

Lopez was born on February 23, 1975, in Manhattan, to Frank and Katherine Lopez. By one published biography, his paternal grandfather was Filipino and his paternal grandmother was of Filipino and Scottish American heritage. He learned piano as a child and studied English at Yale, graduating in 1997.

His first big hit was Avenue Q, a puppet musical for adults created with Jeff Marx, which won the 2004 Tony Awards for Best Musical and Best Original Score. He then co-created The Book of Mormon with Trey Parker and Matt Stone, which opened on Broadway in 2011 and won the Tony for Best Musical. He won two Daytime Emmys for the children's series The Wonder Pets. With Anderson-Lopez he wrote the songs for Disney's Frozen. "Let It Go" won the Oscar in 2014 and made him, at 39, the youngest person at the time to complete an EGOT.
keyFacts: 2011: The Book of Mormon opened on Broadway.
2018: Oscar for "Remember Me"; first double EGOT.
people.connectToWork: What does your form or your first impression assume about a person's heritage from a last name, and how would you ask instead?

sources.label: Yale Schwarzman Center, Kristen Anderson-Lopez and Robert Lopez '97

photo.alt: Robert Lopez, at left in a black suit and purple tie, smiling beside Kristen Anderson-Lopez in a black dress at a theater event.

people.name: Kay Ulanday Barrett
body: Kay Ulanday Barrett is a poet, performer and essayist. The Foundation for Contemporary Arts describes them as navigating life in the U.S. as a disabled, Filipinx-American, transgender queer person. They were born in Mackinaw City, Michigan, earned a B.A. in Gender and Women's Studies at DePaul University, and live in Rahway, New Jersey.

Their first poetry collection, When the Chant Comes, came out from Topside Press in 2016. Their second, More Than Organs (Sibling Rivalry Press, 2020), was a 2021 American Library Association Stonewall Honor Book and a 2021 Lambda Literary Award finalist. They won the 2022 Cy Twombly Award for Poetry, and in July 2024 the Ford and Mellon foundations named them a Disability Futures Fellow. Barrett uses the identity-first word disabled, and their writing and teaching center disability justice.
people.connectToWork: When a person has intersecting identities or access needs, can staff coordinate support across services, or does the process require separate explanations at each step?

people.name: Erick Marco Ramos
body: Indiana University of Pennsylvania reported in December 2023 that Erick Marco Ramos, a Fulbright Scholar and English Ph.D. candidate, has been blind since birth and is from the Philippines. He was interviewed by the American Council of the Blind after receiving one of its scholarships, and he was the first person featured in its Scholarship Spotlight series.

His research in art and literature draws on his own experience of disability. He is an active member of Blind Pride International and hopes to foster inclusion and connection across identities in the U.S. and in his native Philippines.
keyFacts: December 2023: English Ph.D. candidate at Indiana University of Pennsylvania.
American Council of the Blind scholarship recipient.

institutions.name: Fil-Minnesotan Association
institutions.location: Based in Plymouth, by MNopedia's account; serves the Twin Cities and beyond
body: In 1953, twelve Filipino students at the University of Minnesota started meeting to share companionship, news from home and Filipino food. Led by René Dawis and Lily Salcedo, they wrote a constitution and came to call their group the Fil-Minnesotan Association.

As more Filipino doctors, nurses and other professionals settled in Minnesota from the 1960s on, the group grew. In 1966, under Dr. Emmanuel Balcos, it began raising money for a Filipiniana collection at the University of Minnesota Library. In 1976 Abe Malicsi started Paskong Pilipino, a Christmas celebration for children. It staged original musicals such as Ngalan Mo'y Pilipino (1989) and MUSIKAL!, which premiered at the World Theater in St. Paul in 1995.

It also took on the needs of families. It held parent-youth seminars, which led to a Fil-Minnesotan Youth group, ran free health screening clinics, raised money for victims of the Mount Pinatubo eruption, and in 1992 helped the Children's Heart Fund set up a cardiac center for children in the Philippines. In 2008 President Darwin Yasis introduced four pillars: Arts and Culture, Akademy (education), Helping Hands and Community Development. In 2009 it established the Philippine Center of Minnesota in Maplewood. As of October 2026 it holds two seats on the center's board.
keyFacts: 1953: Founded by 12 Filipino students at the University of Minnesota.
2009: Established the Philippine Center of Minnesota.

institutions.name: Philippine Center of Minnesota
body: In 2009, the Fil-Minnesotan Association established a building at 1380 Frost Avenue in Maplewood and called it a "home away from home." The IRS had granted the Philippine Center of Minnesota its tax exemption in July 2003.

On its GiveMN page, the center describes its purpose as giving a gathering place to more than 24,000 Filipino Americans in Minnesota, preserving culture and heritage, and offering social, educational and preventive services for new immigrants, seniors and youth. Its site lists event halls and conference rooms for rent, volunteer work, and a list of Filipino community organizations. Its board includes representatives of ten of those groups.

The Philippine Consulate General in Chicago, which serves Minnesota, has held outreach events at the center, including an April 20, 2024, mission for passport, dual citizenship and other services, by appointment.
keyFacts: Keeps a list of Filipino community organizations.
institutions.connectToWork: If your team wants to meet people at a place they already use, who would you ask first, what do you bring, and who pays for the space and time?

sources.label: Philippine Consulate General in Chicago, Minnesota outreach notice
ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, Philippine Center of Minnesota

photo.alt: Event hall set for a banquet, with round tables in white and gold and light blue balloon arrangements on tall stands.

institutions.name: Filipino American National Historical Society
body: In 1982, Dorothy Laigo Cordova founded the Filipino American National Historical Society in Seattle, and her husband, Fred Cordova, became its founding president and archivist. The Cordovas, who had organized Filipino Youth Activities in Seattle since 1957, set out to collect a history that was barely in textbooks.

In 1987 the society created the National Pinoy Archives at its Seattle office. Pinoy is an informal word Filipinos use for themselves. The archives hold clippings, photographs and transcribed oral histories from families across the country. NBC News reported in October 2016 that the society's National Museum was set to open in downtown Stockton, California, a historic center of Filipino American farm labor.

In 1992 the society began commemorating October as Filipino American History Month, and on November 2, 2009, the U.S. House of Representatives passed a resolution recognizing it. The society says it has more than 40 chapters. Its list shows none in Minnesota; the nearest current chapters listed include Wisconsin and Greater Chicago. Its 2026 national conference, its first in the Washington, D.C., area, drew more than 400 people, and its 2026 history month theme centers intersectional Filipino American histories.
keyFacts: 1992: Began commemorating Filipino American History Month in October.
institutions.connectToWork: Whose stories does your organization record, and whose are lost when people retire or die? What would it take to record them with consent?

institutions.name: Filipino-American Association for Developmental Disabilities
body: The Filipino-American Association for Developmental Disabilities supports Filipino Americans with developmental disabilities and their families in the San Diego area. Its activities include family camps, summer picnics, holiday parties, and workshops on topics such as self-determination and National Core Indicators. It also acts as a link between families and service providers.

Its website shows religious and cultural events alongside this work, including a 2025 Flores de Mayo and Santacruzan. As of October 2026 it lists a member meeting by Zoom on October 26 and a Christmas party in National City, California, on December 13. It is not in Minnesota, and no Filipino disability organization in Minnesota was found.
keyFacts: Serves people with developmental disabilities and their families.
Holds family camps, picnics and workshops.
institutions.connectToWork: Where do families you work with already share disability information with one another, and how could your program support that without taking it over?

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Filipino means people with roots in the Philippines, who differ widely by generation, region of origin, faith, education, language and time in the U.S. Published research on Filipino Americans and disability is thin. Most of what was found concerns mental health, older adults or autism and comes from California or from curriculum material. No Minnesota study was found.
questions: How do you and your family describe what's going on? What words feel respectful to you?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Who gave it, and has it helped or got in the way?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Who in your family usually helps make decisions about care? Would you like them included, and is there anything you want to decide on your own?
What language do you prefer for meetings and written materials: English, Tagalog or another language?
Are there faith practices, church supports or home remedies that are part of your care? How can our services fit with them?
What times work for appointments? Do family members who help have work schedules we should plan around?
Would you like to be connected with other families or a community group, or would you rather keep this private?
Is there anything you'd want to share about how this came about? You don't have to answer.

context.heading: Explanations of illness and disability in the sources found
body: Stanford University's ethnogeriatrics curriculum has a Filipino module on older adults and mental illness. It is teaching material, not a study, with no sample of its own, and the page shows no date. It says some older adults may see mental illness as a weak spirit or as punishment for wrongdoing, and it describes bahala na as a way of coping that leaves illness to God's will. It says such patterns can help people adjust at first and can also delay treatment. It also notes that faith helps people cope. It says some older adults may discuss their concern with a trusted relative, friend, spiritual counselor or healer, may use traditional home remedies, and may avoid mental health services for fear of ridicule.

A 2015 conference abstract by Sharee Anzaldo at UCLA describes a planned interview study of Filipino American parents of autistic children. It reports no findings and no sample size. It frames health as balance, timbang, as background. A 2021 column by Allyx Formalejo, a caregiver in the Philippines, quotes one reader who said disability can be seen as the work of evil rather than a medical condition. That is one person's report from the Philippines, not U.S. research. None of this tells you what any person thinks. Ask.

sources.label: Stanford University, Ethnogeriatrics curriculum, Filipino module, Health Behaviors
Anzaldo (UCLA School of Nursing), Parenting a Child with Autism: Filipino American Beliefs and Perceptions, conference abstract (2015)
Formalejo, Where Are the Voices of Filipino PWDs? Hemophilia News Today (2021)

context.heading: Family, disclosure and getting help
body: The Stanford module says families can strongly shape care decisions, that a person may defer to an authoritative family member to keep harmony, and that some first seek advice from relatives or friends who work in health care. It names hiya (shame) and amor propio (sensitivity to criticism) as reasons some older adults may hold back from disclosing mental illness. The Anzaldo abstract names the same two terms along with pakikisama (getting along) and bahala na as values that may shape help-seeking. These words are ideas from the sources, not labels for people.

Hear the person directly, even if family speaks first. Because disagreeing may be hard for anyone in a meeting with an official, ask open questions and check understanding by having the person explain the plan back, rather than asking whether they understand.
In the Philippines, Formalejo reports that some people hide conditions to keep their jobs. This is not U.S. data, but it can help you explain clearly what is shared, with whom and why.

sources.label: Stanford University, Ethnogeriatrics curriculum, Filipino module, Health Behaviors
Anzaldo (UCLA School of Nursing), Parenting a Child with Autism: Filipino American Beliefs and Perceptions, conference abstract (2015)
Formalejo, Where Are the Voices of Filipino PWDs? Hemophilia News Today (2021)

context.heading: System barriers to check first
body: The Stanford module names practical barriers: few culturally oriented services, limited awareness of services, financial and environmental needs that come first, and working adult family members who cannot attend during usual hours. Check these before reading a missed appointment as cultural. Offer flexible times and say plainly that services are confidential.

sources.label: Stanford University, Ethnogeriatrics curriculum, Filipino module, Health Behaviors

context.heading: Language, interpreters and words
body: Some people prefer English and some prefer Tagalog or another Philippine language, so ask rather than assume either way. Use trained interpreters, not children or relatives, for anything clinical or legal, and confirm the interpreter's language matches the person's.

No documented list of Tagalog disability terms, or of which ones carry stigma, was found. PWD, for person with disability, is in common use in the Philippines, by Formalejo's account. Kay Ulanday Barrett uses the identity-first word disabled. Follow each person's own preference.

sources.label: Formalejo, Where Are the Voices of Filipino PWDs? Hemophilia News Today (2021)
Foundation for Contemporary Arts, Kay Ulanday Barrett

context.heading: Strengths and what could not be found
body: The people profiled above include disabled Filipino leaders, artists and scholars: Kay Ulanday Barrett and Erick Marco Ramos. The Filipino-American Association for Developmental Disabilities shows one group's model of family camps, picnics and faith events used to share information.

No Minnesota research on Filipino Americans and disability was found, and no Filipino disability organization in Minnesota. The Philippine Nurses Association of Minnesota and the Philippine Center of Minnesota may know more locally.

communityRoutes.name: Philippine Center of Minnesota
communityRoutes.purpose: Maplewood community center with a list of Filipino community organizations, including nurses, physicians and a seniors' group. It is not a disability service, but it can help you find who to talk to.

communityRoutes.name: Filipino-American Association for Developmental Disabilities
communityRoutes.purpose: California family group for people with developmental disabilities. It holds member meetings by Zoom, and could be a peer contact for a Minnesota family that wants one. Check whether it takes members from outside its area.

organizations.intro: Filipino Minnesotans have organized since 1953, starting with University of Minnesota students. Minnesota Compass, using 2020–2024 survey data, estimates 26,559 Filipino people in the state, give or take 2,422, with about 71 percent in the Twin Cities and about 42 percent foreign-born; the Council on Asian Pacific Minnesotans gave 22,437 in 2023. Counts differ by source and method. The Philippine Center of Minnesota keeps a list of groups, and no current Minnesota Filipino newspaper was found. These are starting points for learning. The list is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.name: Cultural Society of Filipino Americans of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Founded September 17, 1972. MNopedia describes the Pamana Dance Troupe, Philippine Day, Pasko sa Nayon, children's camps, free Tagalog classes since 2018 and a Disaster Relief Fund. Its Facebook page is listed on the Philippine Center's directory, and it holds two seats on the center's board.

entries.name: Philippine Nurses Association of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Professional association for Filipino nurses in Minnesota. It filed its 2025 federal return in August 2026 and holds two seats on the Philippine Center's board.

entries.name: Philippine Minnesotan Medical Association
entries.purpose: Physicians in Minnesota with ties to the Filipino community. It holds two seats on the Philippine Center's board. It has a Facebook page, linked from the directory.

entries.name: Foundation for Philippine Medical Missions
entries.purpose: Established in Minnesota in 2017. Provides free medical services to communities in the Philippines. Lists a February 2027 mission in Prosperidad, Agusan del Sur.

entries.name: Filipino American Women's Network of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Women's network listed on the Philippine Center's directory, with two seats on its board. It has a Facebook page, linked from the directory.

entries.name: Filipinx for Immigrant Rights & Racial Justice Minnesota
entries.purpose: By its own description, a nonprofit, nonpartisan group founded in 2016 by Filipinx community leaders in response to anti-immigrant rhetoric. It holds two seats on the Philippine Center's board.

entries.name: Minnesota Filipino Seniors' Association
entries.purpose: Seniors' group listed on the Philippine Center's directory. It has a Facebook page, linked from the directory. Nothing was found showing it runs disability programs.

entries.name: University of the Philippines Alumni in Minnesota
entries.purpose: Alumni network with two seats on the Philippine Center's board. It has a Facebook page, linked from the directory.

entries.name: Philippine Study Group of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Says it educates and advocates for social justice and funds grassroots projects, and calls itself the last group remaining of those formed against the Marcos dictatorship. Its site's latest dated items are from 2019, and it holds two seats on the Philippine Center's board.

entries.name: Filipino Catholic Church
entries.purpose: Listed on the Philippine Center's directory, with two seats on its board. The directory does not yet give a profile, parish or website.

entries.name: Philippine Student Association, University of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Student group listed by the university's Asian American Studies program among the organizations it works with.
entries.linkLabel: University of Minnesota list of student organizations

entries.name: Filipino-American National News, KFAI
entries.location: Minneapolis and St. Paul, 90.3 FM and online
entries.purpose: Weekly Sunday program at 9 p.m. with Filipino news, music, community events and interviews, hosted by Alan Bungue. Latest episode listed October 25, 2026.

entries.name: Asian American Press
entries.purpose: No longer publishing. Its site is a digital archive of the pan-Asian Minnesota paper, 1982 to the 2020s, founded by Nghi Huynh. Useful for past Filipino community stories.

entries.name: National Federation of Filipino American Associations
entries.purpose: Founded in 1997. Calls itself the largest national affiliation of Filipino American institutions. Works on civic engagement and policy; held its 2026 national conference in Aurora, Colorado. A Minnesota chapter was not confirmed.

entries.name: Philippine Nurses Association of America
entries.location: National, based in North Brunswick, New Jersey
entries.purpose: National professional body for Filipino American nurses, with regional chapters and more than four decades of work by its own account. Lists its 48th national convention.

entries.name: Filipino Young Leaders Program
entries.purpose: Founded in 2012. A network of Filipino diaspora leaders; runs a 2026 immersion program in the Philippines and the Tayo initiative.

entries.name: National Filipino American Lawyers Association
entries.purpose: Says it is the national voice of the Filipino American legal profession, advocating for justice, civil rights and equal opportunity. Associate organization of the National Asian Pacific American Bar Association, with a 2026 leadership summit.

entries.name: Association of Philippine Physicians in America
entries.purpose: Established in 1972; now calls itself the National Organization of Filipino American Physicians. Its goals include continuing education, medical research and free care for people with low incomes.

entries.name: Asian Journal
entries.purpose: National Filipino American news, in English. It covered Justice Aligada's appointment in 2026.

entries.name: The FilAm
entries.purpose: Magazine for Filipino Americans in New York that also covers national news, with posts through October 2026. There is no evidence of how widely it is read in Minnesota.

entries.name: The Filipino Channel
entries.purpose: Philippine news, dramas and entertainment for Filipinos abroad, in Filipino and English.

entries.name: GMA Pinoy TV
entries.purpose: Philippine news and entertainment for overseas Filipinos. GMA announced its launch on YouTube TV in the U.S. in 2024.

entries.name: Philippine Daily Inquirer
entries.purpose: National Philippine news in English, updated through October 2026.

entries.name: Rappler
entries.purpose: Philippine and world news and investigations in English and Filipino.
